sections.h2: What speeds up a house sale in Queensbury?
sections.html:
Knowing the tax calendar and the permit history before a buyer asks, then choosing a buyer whose closing does not depend on a lender. A cash purchase skips appraisal and underwriting, while the deed and town records follow the usual path.

Queensbury is a first-class town in Warren County, in the southern Adirondack foothills. It covers 62.80 square miles of land and wraps the city of Glens Falls on three sides. A house here might sit near Lake George, in West Glens Falls or on a rural road, and the school district and fire district on your bills depend on where it is.

Four school districts cover the town: Queensbury Union Free, Glens Falls City, Hudson Falls Central and Lake George Central. Your school tax bill names yours, and a listing should too, since buyers ask about it first.

Five fire protection districts operate here: Bay Ridge, North Queensbury, Queensbury Central, South Queensbury and West Glens Falls. Hamlets include Glen Lake, West Glens Falls, Kattskill Bay, East Lake George, Oneida Corners and Harrisena.

Lake George forms the northern edge of town and the Hudson River runs along the southern boundary. Parts of the western and northern town fall inside the Adirondack Park, which can add permit conditions to a parcel. The town has had no police force of its own since 1982, so the Warren County Sheriff's Office and the State Police cover it.

Queensbury leans toward ownership and toward older residents. Owners live in 75.5% of the homes, and 25.9% of residents are 65 or older. With a population of 29,049, the town is steady rather than growing fast.

sections.h2: Buildings and Codes before a sale
sections.html:
The Town of Queensbury's Buildings and Codes office is where you ask about permits and certificates of occupancy. The planning and zoning offices handle land use questions.

Ask whether your house has a certificate of occupancy on file for every addition, whether any permits are still open, and whether the town expects any inspection or certificate in connection with the transfer. Put these questions to the office early. A missing certificate for a finished attic or garage conversion is the kind of gap that delays a closing.

A house on septic raises more questions. New York's disclosure form asks for the system's age, the date of the last pumping and how often it is pumped, so dig those records out before listing. The same form covers flood zones, wetlands, agricultural districts and fuel tanks, all common on lakeside or rural lots.

Warren County's Real Property Tax Services publishes the yearly calendar Queensbury follows. Around September 1 most school district bills go out, and around January 1 most municipal bills do, each with 30 days free of interest. New purchasers are told to contact both the school and municipal tax collectors so a bill is not missed.

  • March 1: Taxable Status Date and the deadline to file any exemption, new or renewal, with the Assessor.
  • April 1: all outstanding taxes become county liens payable to the county Treasurer.
  • May 1: tentative roll filed and change-of-assessment notices mailed.
  • Fourth Tuesday in May: Grievance Day, when the Board of Assessment Review hears assessment complaints.
  • July 1: assessments become final and are used for the coming year's taxes.

April 1 is the date that surprises sellers. Once a bill has moved to the county, the payoff must come from the county Treasurer rather than the town tax receiver, so have your attorney order the right figure.

sections.h2: Warren County Clerk fees for a deed
sections.html:
The Warren County Clerk records deeds at the municipal center on U.S. Route 9, south of the village of Lake George. The fee schedule lists $40 a document, $5 for the cover sheet, $5 a page, $5 for the TP-584, and $125 for the RP-5217 on qualifying residential or farm property ($250 for other property). Residential deeds also carry a $10 notice of conveyance fee.

State transfer tax is $4.00 per $1,000, with nothing due at $500 or less. Recording and filing are open from 8:00 a.m. until 3:30 p.m., and electronic recording is available. The clerk's office also records Adirondack Park Agency permits, so look for permit conditions on any parcel inside the Park before closing.

A short list saves the most time. Pull the school and town tax bills, find any certificates of occupancy, and note when the septic system or well was last serviced. Near Lake George or inside the Adirondack Park, also check recorded documents for easements or permit conditions a buyer will want to see.

Then choose a route. A standard listing reaches owner-occupant buyers but relies on inspections and a mortgage approval. A cash sale closes without a lender. Both end at the county clerk, whose recording window closes at 3:30 p.m., so plan signing times around it.

If taxes are owed when you sell, the closing attorney pays them from the proceeds. After April 1, ask the county Treasurer for the payoff figure rather than the town.

sections.h2: From accepted offer to recorded deed
sections.html:
The order of events is about the same whichever buyer you pick. Once you sign a contract, the buyer's attorney will order title work and ask for the town file: certificates of occupancy, open permits and any septic records. Your attorney requests tax payoff figures from the school and town collectors, or from the county Treasurer once April 1 is behind you.

At closing you sign the deed, the TP-584 transfer tax form and the RP-5217 transfer report. The deed then goes to the Warren County Clerk, where the $4.00 per $1,000 transfer tax is collected with the recording fees. Electronic recording is available, which helps when the filing window is tight.

With a cash buyer the lender steps drop out, so there is no appraisal to wait on and no mortgage commitment that can fall through. The title, tax and permit steps above still apply, which is why gathering those papers first is the most useful thing you can do. If you have an exemption on your bill, remember the buyer must file their own by March 1 to keep one.

faqs.q: How do I tell which school district my Queensbury house is in?
faqs.a: Your school tax bill names it. Four districts share the town: Queensbury Union Free, Glens Falls City, Hudson Falls Central and Lake George Central.

faqs.q: What is the Queensbury tax mailing schedule?
faqs.a: Most school bills are mailed near September 1 and most municipal bills near January 1, each with 30 interest-free days. Anything unpaid becomes a county lien on April 1.

faqs.q: What does recording a Warren County deed cost?
faqs.a: Budget $40 per document plus $5 for the cover sheet, $5 a page, $5 for the TP-584 and $125 for the RP-5217 on qualifying residential property.

faqs.q: Does a parcel inside the Adirondack Park change the sale?
faqs.a: The Warren County Clerk records Adirondack Park Agency permits. Ask whether any permit is recorded against your parcel and give it to the buyer's attorney.

faqs.q: What is Grievance Day in Queensbury?
faqs.a: It falls on the fourth Tuesday in May, when the Board of Assessment Review hears assessment complaints. Exemption filings are due to the Assessor by March 1.
